corrected_value.title: Frequency of word-use predicts rates of lexical evolution throughout Indo-European history

decisions.quote:
We have previously shown that the ‘low limit’ number words (from one to five) have exceptionally slow rates
6    of lexical replacement when measured across the Indo-European languages. Here we replicate this finding
7    within the Bantu and Austronesian language families, and with new data for the Indo-European languages.
decisions.location: Summary, page 2, lines 164-166 (see also Introduction, page 2, lines 179-180, 198-218; References, page 10, lines 918-920)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study: Pagel, Atkinson & Meade (2007), 'Frequency of word-use predicts rates of lexical evolution throughout Indo-European history' (Reference [1]). The Summary and Introduction explicitly state that this paper replicates and extends their previous finding [1] on the exceptionally slow lexical replacement rates of low-limit number words (one to five). Other works cited for supplying lexical/phylogenetic datasets ([3], [11], [12]) or for background explanatory context (such as Zipf [28]) are not re-tested target findings.

decisions.quote:
We have previously shown that the ‘low limit’ number words (from one to five) have exceptionally slow rates
6    of lexical replacement when measured across the Indo-European languages. Here we replicate this finding
7    within the Bantu and Austronesian language families, and with new data for the Indo-European languages.
8    Number words can remain stable for 10,000 to over 100,000 years, or around 3.5 to 20 times longer than
9    average rates of lexical replacement among the Swadesh list of ‘fundamental vocabulary’ items.
decisions.location: Summary, page 2, lines 164-168 (see also Results 3(a)-(b), pages 5-6, lines 472-475, 554-563; Discussion, page 9, lines 807-814)
decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall verdict that they replicate the original finding from Pagel, Atkinson & Meade (2007) [1] across the Bantu and Austronesian language families and with new Indo-European data. In the Results and Discussion, they confirm that low-limit number words fall at the slowest end of lexical replacement rate distributions across all three language families (3.5 to 20 times slower than average Swadesh items) and that the new Indo-European rates correlate at r = 0.91 with the 2007 study.

decisions.location: Summary, page 2, lines 164-166 (see also Introduction, page 3, lines 253-258; Materials and Methods, page 3, lines 264-270)
decisions.reason: The study uses new language datasets and samples (Bantu, Austronesian, an expanded 103-language Indo-European dataset, and Pama-Nyungan rank-order data) to re-test the previously published finding of Pagel, Atkinson & Meade (2007) [1] that low-limit number words have exceptionally slow rates of lexical replacement, which qualifies as a replication under the codebook.
